1.	Did the Right Honourable, the Prime Minister, when leader of the Opposition, make the following statement at Halifax:
" A thorough and complete reformation of the laws relating to the Civil Service should be put into effect, so that future appointments shall be made by an independent commission acting upon the report of examiners after competitive examination. I am convincecb-that we shall perform a great public duty by establishing in this country that system which prevails in Great Britain, under which a member of Parliament has practically no voice in or control over any appointment to the Civil Service.
" To use the power of filling positions in the public service as a reward for party service and without regard to the character and capacity of the individual selected, is a gross breach of a solemn public trust. A private trustee so dishonouring his office would be subject to punishment by the criminal law."
2.	If so, what was the object of making such a statement?
3.	Have any appointments to the Civil Service been made since October, 1911? If so, how many?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1.	The language quoted consists of certain statements detached from their context hut is substantially correct.
2.	To impress the importance of the subject upon the people and upon the Government then in power. The purpose had considerable success as the then Government within a few months thereafter introduced the reforms effected by the Civil Service Act of 1908.
3.	Appointments have been made to the Civil Service since October, 1911. A return to he brought down as soon as the necessary information has been compiled will indicate the number.
4.	Appointments to the inside service are made upon the certificate of the Civil Service Commission under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Appointments to the outside service are made upon the responsibility of the Government and after careful inquiry as to the character and capacity of the individual selected. For the purpose of obtaining such information the Government is ready to receive assistance from members of Parliament or from other persons who are capable of giving reliable information as to such character and capacity. The recommendation of a member of Parliament or any other person is not alone or of itself sufficient for the appointment of a public officer, as character and capacity must be taken into consideration by the Government.
5.	The public steps which have been taken by the Prime Minister are within the knowledge of the bon. member asking the question, as they are on record in Parliament. As to other steps which have not yet been made public, any necessary announcement will be made in due course.

Mr. G. W. KYTE (Richmond, N.S.) asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing the question of the postal service in Nova Scotia.
And leave having been granted,
He said: For some weeks great complaints have been made with respect to the carriage and delivery of mails in the constituency which I represent, and in other constituencies as well. The hon. Postmaster General a few evenings ago in discussing the work of his department explained the development which has taken place in the postal service of the Dominion of Canada during the last three or four years. The expenditure in respect of that service now amounts to $13,000,000 a year. The report of the Postmaster General for the fiscal year ended March 31 last disclosed the fact that a great many rural delivery routes and other conveniences have been established throughout the Dominion of Canada. I respectfully submit that we in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia do not participate in these additional conveniences which are enjoyed in the other sections of Canada. If confidence in the postal service is withdrawn, the very foundations of civil life are shaken. I have here a letter which
I received a few days ago from an official in the province of Nova Scotia, in which he makes complaint regarding the postal service in the part of the country over which his jurisdiction extends. He says:
I have been the prime mover in the agitation for improvement in our mail accommodation; but, unfortunately, I have had occasion to make so many complaints for some time past of delay and miscarriage of mail, that I have doubtless made myself obnoxious. When I got tired sending complaints to Halifax, I began sending them over their heads to Ottawa and, I am sorry to say, with no better results, until at last I made my bow and retired from the contest, promising not to trouble them any more.
Since I am on the subject, I may as well say that the same causes of complaint continue. There is not a week that mail does not go astray or get delayed en route. Within the last week the Halifax newspapers, on which we depend for the daily news, miscarried twice. The enclosed letter will disclose a flagrant case. I sent a parcel of blank forms of school returns to the teachers at Port Hood for their semi-annual return^. Subsequently, a letter came from the secretary of the school board asking me to forward a set of blanks, which I did. Some days afterwards a telegram comes, asking why I did not send the required forms. The third consignment reaches in due course, and, as you will see by Mr. Murphy's letter, the other two parcels came sauntering leisurely along some days later.
Would my hon. friend give the name?

I shall be very glad to give the name to the Postmaster General. I do not think it desirable to enter the names of private citizens upon the published records of Parliament. Another gentleman in the county which I have the honour to represent, and to whom I had arranged that Hansard for this session should be sent daily, writes:
I have not received a copy of Hansard the last two weeks, and I have received but four copies in all since Parliament opened.
Parliament opened on the 4th day of February last. As I said, I had made arrangements to have a copy of Hansard sent to this gentleman daily; but up to the date on which he wrote, the 5th of March, he had received only four copies and had not received a copy for two weeks. Another gentleman for whom I had made a similar arrangement writes me that up to the 15th of February he had not received a single copy of Hansard from the Printing Bureau. I may say, in justice to the officers of the Printing Bureau, that before I thought of bringing this matter before the House I communicated with them and they satisfied me that the failure to deliver Hansard to the gentlemen to whom I refer cannot be traceable to them as they gave satisfactory proofs that they mailed

Hansard every day. I have another ease which affects myself more particularly, and as it does affect me more particularly I regard it as the most serious case of all. On the 11th day of January last I wrote a letter addressed to my hon. friend for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). That letter should have reached him on the evening of the 11th day of January. On the 15th day of January he wired me asking why I had not sent him the letter which he expected.
I communicated the non-delivery of this letter to the post office inspector at Halifax, who immediately undertook to trace it, hut up to the present hour without success. This is quite easily understood as the letter was not registered and there was no way in which it could be traced through the various post offices that it would pass through en route. Suffice it to say that this letter, which was an important communication and one which I was very desirous should reach my hon. friend in due course of mail, has not yet come into his hands. Another letter which I addressed to him on the following day which should have reached Mm on the 12th day of January did not reach him until the 16th, some four days afterwards, and the delay in that case was caused by the letter having been mis-sent in another direction to another post office. These matters are too important to be allowed to continue and, while I have no reflections to make upon the hon. gentleman who is now discharging the important duties of Postmaster General, I am bound to say that the conditions which we have at present are those which he inherited from a not over punctilious predecessor. From time to time in this House, members representing the party to which I am associated have felt called upon to protest against the numerous changes of postmasters in the province of Nova Scotia. For many years we had a system of post offices that were in charge of postmasters who had served a considerable time in those offices and who, by training and experience, were calculated to give every possible satisfaction. After the change of Government there was a demand for the universal dismissal and official execution of these postmasters, particularly those who happened to he in sympathy with the late Government. As a consequence of this demand these competent and well trained officials have been dismissed from office and a band of men quite untrained and unqualified has taken their places. In so far as this is a reflection upon the Government I am willing that that impression may remain. I think it is too bad,
however, that the public service should suffer in the manner I have described. I would urge the Postmaster General to take such steps as will give us some reasonable assurance that the postal service will be *conducted more satisfactorily in the future.
I know of one case where a man living in my community, having undergone a serious surgical operation in an hospital in a neighbouring county, on his return found it *necessary to communicate with the medical man under whose treatment he was. He addressed three letters to the medical man in question, none of which had reached its destination upon the 30th day of January at the time I left home, notwithstanding that the letters had been written some two or three weeks before and should have reached their destination within 24 hours. There is another case of a woman living in my neighbourhood who suffered for many weeks from a serious illness by which she was reduced from comparative affluence and comfort to a condition of great distress. A friend of hers sent a generous benefaction to her by letter addressed to the post office where she received her mail. This letter was not received, and when inquiries were especially made it was found that this letter remained in the post office for four weeks, notwithstanding that the person to whom it waa addressed had every day sent messengers to that office for her mail. I know other instances which I would be glad to discuss with the Postmaster General which would seem to indioate that there are grounds for public confidence in postal service being weakened. I fear very much that there are some postmasters who have an idea that, since their friends are in power and they have been selected to fill these offices on account of party services rendered by them, they are at liberty to set at defiance certain rules and regulations which heretofore have been regarded as binding. I fear that there is not that secrecy existing in the post offices in some places in Nova Scotia that it is necessary and desirable should exist. I know cases where persons not at all connected or associated with the post office staff have the run of post offices in some small centres, and no person mailing letters at these post offices has the assurance that the addresses, if not the contents of the letters, will not be disclosed to those who have an interest in ascertaining this information. If reports be true, we are upon the eve of a general election in this country, Important confidential correspondence in re-

lation to the election campaign must necessarily pass through post offices. I take the responsibility of saying here to-day that there are certain post offices in my county where I would not take the risk of mailing confidential correspondence during an election campaign. I desire to make this statement in order that the Postmaster General may make a note of it, and issue warnings to these postmasters that the public have a right to repose some confidence in their discharge of their duties, and that no trifling with the mails will be permitted. I know of an instance where, in a municipal election campaign, certain correspondence was supposed to have been de-posted in the post office upon the eve of that election. On the day subsequent to that, a day when the post office was not supposed to be open, two persons not associated with the post office were seen coming out of it, one of whom shut the door as he came out and put the key in his pocket. That information satisfied me that in this particular case the public interest is not safeguarded, and a proper appreciation of his obligation is not felt by the postmaster. I have information to the effect that in another election campaign in this country some two years ago, not in the province of Nova Scotia, 90 per cent of the campaign literature which was mailed in certain post offices in one constituency was never delivered to the persons to whom it was addressed.
The statements which I make here this afternoon are made in absolute good faith, and with a full knowledge of the responsibility which should rest on any hon. member who undertakes to make such statements in this House. But I repeat that, in addition to the specific complaints which I have made this afternoon, there are many others which I might very well bring to the attention of this House; but I do not desire to delay the proceedings. All I ask at the present moment is that the hon. Postmaster General will give such instructions to his inspectors as will enable them to ferret out the cause of the non-delivery of the mail in the instances I have referred to, and in those instructions give a warning that postmasters cannot in future interfere with the mails and letters passing through their offices without running the risk of being summarily punished for such an offence, even though they have been appointed to their offices by the hon. gentlemen at present occupying the Treasury benches.
I should like to ask the hon. member whether the late Government, when they came into power in 1896, did not dismiss competent men and put incompetent men in their places?

I can only speak of knowledge concerning my own constituency; and with respect to my own constituency I desire to tell my hon. friend that from 1896 to 1911 not one postmaster was dismissed in the county of Richmond, which I represent. Every man who had been appointed by the Conservative Government previous to 1896 was continued in his office, and he has continued to hold up to the present moment.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
I have much pleasure in confirming, as far as my personal knowledge goes, the observations made by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte). I think his observations in bringing this matter to the notice of the Postmaster General ought to be of some service, and ought to bring into existence such a condition of affairs between the postmasters and the department that the postmasters should know that they are not to be at all events encouraged in conduct of that kind. I wish to say to the Postmaster General that to my knowledge the post office in the Tory centres in the part of eastern Nova Scotia that I know is just a place that is occupied by Tory heelers for their meetings at all hours and at all times, Sundays not excepted. While the Postmaster General cannot follow these men into their offices and see that they take proper care that the letters are not opened or interfered with, there is one thing which I think he can do; and that is to prevent the post office from being a place of common resort of the kind I have mentioned. If the Postmaster General will make inquiry into the situation which I speak of, he will find that in all the villages where changes and new appointments have been made since the last general election, the postmasters think they are there as political agents of their friends, and that the post office is of course the proper place in which to gather and discuss political matters; and if they suspect any letters that may be going through they take such steps as may be advised, in order to obtain the desired information. That is a condition of things that should not exist; it should be removed. A little over a year ago a local election took place in the county of Victoria. The chief

Tory organizer of the province of Nova Scotia, Dr. Hayes, who was on that occasion black-listed and disqualified by the judge of the Supreme Court-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is travelling outside what is permissible on this motion, which is to inquire into the unsatisfactory condition of the postal service now in Nova Scotia.

It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that I have no particular gift by which I can say everything that I have to say in just one word; and that it is necessary for me to make two or three sentences before I come to the real sentence. I was going to say that this man has commandeered the post offices down there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I understood the hon. gentleman correctly, he was speaking of an occurrence that happened over a year ago. Of course he cannot, in that case, be addressing himself to the present condition of the postal service in Nova Scotia.

I think, from the wording,
that the notice is not limited to the present condition of the postal service.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The notice reads:
The unsatisfactory condition of the postal service in Nova Soot la.
I presume that has reference to the present condition.

I submit that the condition of terror under which postmasters are held by Tory officials existed then, and exists now; it is a continuous trespass, as it is known to the law. I submit that we can speak of this condition as having commenced over a year ago, and as having continued to exist up to the present time. I submit that it is quite proper to go back, if we can, to the origin of the disease, and follow it up to its present stage. I submit that that was the condition over a year ago, and that it is the condition now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that my ruling ought to be respected. A notice worded as this is must be taken as referring to the present.

I say that this condition exists by reason of the interference of Tory officials in the county of Victoria. I say that the chief official of the Tory party in the county, who is the chief adviser of the Premier in Tory matters in that province, a man who has been blacklisted by a judge of the Supreme Court, terrorizes and
commandeers the post offices, and that in the county of Victoria or any other place where he is doing this you cannot get a postmaster to do his duty; for this man goes about telling them he is authorized by the department at Ottawa to dismiss them if they do not carry out his behests. That is the condition, and if I am not to speak of it as in the past I bring the conditions as in the present to the notice of the Postmaster General, so that he may deal with it. I wish to keep strictly within the motion that is before the Chair, but I did not know that it contained a word which restricts us to the very present. I submit to the Postmaster General and to the Government that not only the post office, but every other public service or utility in Nova Scotia, including the telegraph service, is being dealt with in the same way. They commandeered the telegraph service at that election. Thousands of messages were sent out and the minister knows they were not paid for. The man in charge, who is still in the service of the Government, swore that he put those messages through free, without a cent being paid, and he is still the man to whom we must go for our telegrams in the county of Victoria. The condition being such as this man has sworn to himself, I submit to the Postmaster General that he cannot -be too severe in dealing with matters of that kind.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton):
speechtext:
I do not wish to take part in this discussion except to corroborate something that has been said by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). In the first or second week of January last I had occasion to write to the hon. member for Richmond on a matter of importance not only to ourselves personally, but to a large number of other people. In the ordinary course of mail I should have had a reply to my letter on the 12th or 13th of January. On the 14th or 15th of January, not having received a reply I telegraphed the hon. member for Richmond to ascertain why he had mot answered my letter, and in regard to certain inquiries I had made with reference to some engagements in which we were both concerned. He telegraphed back that he had answered my letter, and gave me the desired information. My hon. friend also wrote me a letter	on	the	same subject.
While I should have had the letter on the day it was written, I did not receive it for four or five days afterwards owing

to the fact that the postmaster at the place of mailing the letter had sent it to another post office which bore no resemblance either in name, spelling or otherwise, to the place to which the letter had been addressed. I am not making any charges; I do not know who was responsible for this, I do not know whether the person who mislaid this letter did it wilfully or not, but there is some looseness cr laxity certainly in the post office where the matter occurred. There are other instances that affect myself in the matter of sending out literature, but I am not going to make any comment upon them. It may be the fault of nobody. In the county I represent, people are coming and going, it being a great industrial centre. Very often the literature I send out- Hansards and that sort of thing-is returned to me here. I am making no charge, but I wished to corroborate the statement of my hon. friend from Richmond in reference to the two letters that he addressed to me in the month of January.

I thank the hon. member for
Richmond (Mr. Kyte) for having drawn the attention of the House to these matters, which are of considerable importance. I beg to express the regret of the department that he has been put to inconvenience by not having had these letters transmitted through the mails as they should have been. I am a little surprised that any complaints made about the very unsatisfactory manner in which the post office seems to have been conducted in his town have received no answer.
The letter of the official that I read to the House has no reference to the post office in my town. He lives in another part, and his statement has reference to another post office.

I would ask my hon. friend to kindly come to the department and give me further particulars. I cannot punish any of-these men without hearing them; I have to give them fair warning. If it is necessary to hold an investigation, we certainly shall do so. It will be my endeavour to make the postal service as perfect as possible. Anything that money can do to promote that end will be done by the department over which I have the honour to preside.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is a fair conclusion to draw that if anything goes wrong in the ad-

ministration of the post office it is done through intention or design. I have had instances in my own experience which are of a much stronger character than anything which has been mentioned this afternoon, and I have not thought for one moment of attributing the result to any intention to do wrong. I remember about six years ago I sent an important and urgent letter from Halifax to Ottawa. It reached Ottawa nearly three weeks after I had despatched it, having gone to Vancouver and having returned from Vancouver by slow stages. It was important for many reasons that the letter should have reached Ottawa in due course. I did not, however, jump to the conclusion that any Liberal partisan in the post office had done this from design. My hon. friends on the other side seem to have come to an unwarrantable conclusion. During nearly the whole of a year, about five years ago, a business man in the city of Ottawa sent to me almost daily three or four letters which had occupied in their transmission to him two or three times, and sometimes four or five times, the length of time that would have been necessary. I used to forward these communications from this business man to the Postmaster General for the purpose of directing his attention to the unnecessary delay. In a very large country like this such delays will from time to time occur. So far as the aspersions which have been cast on the postmasters of 4 p.m. Nova Scotia are concerned, I regret that hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon should have gone so far as to cast what I believe to be undeserved reproach upon a class of men who, I believe, are inspired by a sincere desire to do their duty. On their behalf, until some definite and concrete case of maladministration is brought to the attention of the Postmaster General and dealt with as it ought to be dealt with, I desire to repudiate any such aspersions on the postmasters of Nova Scotia. I have had experience of them when they were very largely Liberal appointees, and I found no occasion to reproach them then. I think that no greater occasion for reproach is to be found against those who have been appointed by the present Government. I shall make inquiries as to what the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has said in regard to Dr. Hayes, and ascertain what Dr. Hayes has to say in regard to these accusations. They have not been brought to my attention before, but

with all due respect to the hon. member, I venture to think that it will be found he spoke beyond warrant and beyond the limit of what he should have said, when he made these charges against Dr. Hayes this afternoon. So far as the distribution of campaign literature is concerned, I have heard of reproaches of that kind for the last fifteen or seventeen years, and a great many of them when my hon. friends on the other side of the House were responsible for the administration of the Post Office Department. I know that in the election of 1904 my own political friends made the declaration that they verily believed that not more than 25 per cent of the campaign literature which was sent out in very large quantities from Ottawa ever reached the destination for which it was intended. I do not know whether that is the case or not. I simply desire to remind my hon. friend that we have heard a good deal of these charges during the past seventeen years and before we came into power.
Motion to adjourn the House negatived.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) to an article which appears in the Leader-Mail of Granby, of Friday, March 5, 1915. It is also in connection with the post office service, but in this case there are no officials to blame. The statement is as follows:
The morning mail missed the train again on Wednesday. This is a matter which should be taken up vigorously by the Board of Trade. There is too much doing these days to allow us to quietly submit to being without mail for twenty-four hours. There is no good reason why the mail bags should not be brought from the city direct by the Central Vermont. Under existing arrangements they come to Farnham by Canadian Pacific railway and if this train is late the Central Vermont comes along without them. Telephone requests that the bags be put on the freight which follows the passenger train here do not bring any results and we have to wait for the evening train to pick up the bags and bring them along. Will the Granby Board of Trade, which has been suffering from drowsiness lately, kindly wake up and attend to the matter.
Under the present arrangement the town of Granby, with a population of 5,000, receives a closed mail in the morning on the train from Montreal and the registered mail on the evening train. This closed mail [DOT]is placed on the Canadian Pacific railway train at 8.25 in the morning. The mail is thrown off at Farnham and transferred to
a train which leaves Montreal via the Central Vermont at 8.35 a.m. If the Canadian Pacific railway train is fifteen or twenty minutes late in arriving at Farnham, the mail has missed the connection with the Central Vermont train and remains on the station platform during the entire day. I would ask the Postmaster General if some arrangement could not be made by which this morning mail, instead of leaving at 8.25 by the Canadian Pacific railway, could be placed directly on the train which leaves the Bonaventure station at 8.35, and thus save this inconvenience.

I will look into the matter, and if it is possible to remedy the evil I will have it done.
17th NOVA SCOTIA REGIMENT.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have received a telegram from Sir George Perley, which sets forth the substance of General Alderson's reply to Sir George Perley's letter regarding the allegations of Mr. H. C. Crowell. General Alderson states that the only word of truth in the whole article is that Colonel Robertson has been replaced. He further says that all the nonsense about the 17th Battalion being used as scavengers, etc., is pure invention.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

Referring to the following clause in the new proposed taxation, under the heading of Special Taxation:
On every letter and postcard posted in Canada a war stamp of one cent.
Does this clause apply to mail emanating from this House under the frank of hon. members? If not, in my opinion, it should.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will bring my hon. friend's inquiry to the attention of the Minister of Finance, and I will give an answer to-morrow.

Consideration of the proposed motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment of Sir Wilfrid Laurier thereto, resumed from March 10.
Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough):
In the resolution now before the House the Minister of Finance requires to explain

a deficit of $80,000,000. He ought also to deal with the Estimates submitted to the House. Permit me to pick out a couple of sample items such as a new dredging plant for Manitoba and the inspection of pickled fish. When listening to the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, I could not help wondering what the bombardment of Constantinople had to do with a dredging plant for Manitoba or with pickled fish. I was curious to know the purpose of this item of $33,000, to provide a new dredging plant for Manitoba. I did not know that any dredging was required in that province. I made some inquiries, and it was hinted to me that the Minister of Public Works was promoting this scheme, and that his idea was to dredge a track for the prairie schooners in order that there might be facilities afforded to carry cargoes of homestead inspectors for use at the next election. I do not know whether that explanation is the proper one or not; but if it is not it is for the Minister of Public Works to explain.
Not worth while.

Why, let me ask, did not the hon. Finance Minister deal with the questions before the House? It looks to me as if one of those resolutions is kept on the Order Paper in order to reinforce the other.
When the House adjourned last night I was dealing with the question of a pledge given to the people of Canada by the Prime Minister a few days before the last election.
I read the first clause of his manifesto, which -was published on the 15th day of August, in the Montreal Gazette and signed by the Prime Minister. In this pledge he promises on behalf of his party, if elected, a thorough reorganization of the methods by which public expenditure is supervised. That pledge has not been redeemed. I pointed out to the House that there never was a time in the history of this country since the days of Connolly and McGreevy when there was such a lack of supervision of public expenditure as there is to-day. In order to prove my case I produced correspondence laid on the table only a few days ago between the Minister of Finance and the Auditor General. You can see by that correspondence that things went so far and that the expenditure was so loosely made, in one department of the Government at all events, that it became necessary for the Auditor General to step in and stop the payment of the cheques of the Minister of Finance at the banks.
I want to produce another witness, an 
hon. gentleman who supports the Government. I refer to the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. William Smith). You, Mr. Speaker, know that there is in this House no more loyal supporter of the present Administration than the hon. member for South Ontario. It will be conceded that that hon. member would do things for his party that he would not do for himself. He attended a meeting of the Horse Breeders' Association at Toronto, on the 2nd day of February, 19X5. He took occasion to make a speech, and I will read a paragraph from the report of it published in the Toronto Telegram, which I understand is a Conservative journal. Here is what my hon. friend says:
Perhaps the course of the Government has not met with universal satisfaction, and no doubt there is good reason for this. What I am about to say, i say as a supporter of "the Government and with a due sense of the significance of my words. As far as I can see, gentlemen, there is going to be a considerable graft In this business. I fear the tactics we condemned in connection with the Boer war remount purchases are to be repeated. This should not be. Men have been sent out to buy who might play a game of marbles, but who cannot buy horses.
There you have the opinion of a gentleman who is supporting the Government. His opinion was evidently given very reluctantly. He knows what is taking place, because if there is anything he knows well, it is horses. That want of oversight in the purchase of horses was not confined to the province of Ontario. In the province of Nova Scotia there was one gentleman detailed to purchase horses who would also, I have no doubt, be all right at playing marbles. Every one knows that the Militia Department is besieged day after day by contract brokers, patronage hunters, middlemen, and cattle of that character. All you have to do, if you do not know the facts, is to go down to the headquarters of our war department and see for yourself. There you will find them in hordes, like the army worm. I have very much sympathy with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia, who wished that he had the power to turn his quick-firing guns upon them. That is the way the business of this Government is being done in Ottawa; and outside in the rest of Canada the business of the country devolves upon patronage committees. In the town in which I live the recruiting officer could not select a medical doctor to examine the recruits volunteering for service without submitting to the dictation of a patronage committee. That is how the Minister of Finance is standing behind the boys in the

trenches. It makes a man's blood hot to think that at a time like this, when so many of our people are making great sacrifices, when over fifty thousand of the best blood of Canada are risking their lives in the country's service and every day adding to the number, when some twenty thousand of our countrymen are at this moment somewhere in the blood-soaked swamps of Flanders exposed to the hardships and dangers of war for the defence of their country. All honour to them for their patriotism and courage and devotion to duty. But what shall we say of the grafters, and the jobbers, and the patronage hunters who in this hour of their country's need are thinking only of themselves and of what they can steal for their own pockets or for the reptile funds of their party? The Auditor General is the only safeguard we have; and it would appear from the correspondence laid on the table that he is spending a good deal of his time at present looking after the ministers. It is a Godsend for the people of Canada that we have an Auditor General and that he is a man of integrity and courage. Otherwise they would steal the Mace off the table and the carpets off the floor of this Chamber.
I pointed out in connection with the pledge given by my right hon. friend the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) that he stated in his manifesto that a yearly expenditure of $74,000,000 was extravagance beyond all defence. To-day instead of $74,000,000 we have an ordinary controllable expenditure of $140,000,000. Now, Sir, if there was no excuse, no possible defence for an expenditure of $74,000,000 in 1911, when my right hon. friend wrote that manifesto, how can there be any defence to-day for the enormous expenditure of $140,000,000? If there is a defence we should like to hear it. For, I submit, that in the whole course of this debate no one on the other side so far has attempted to make a proper defence on that question. The people are asking throughout the country, Could this staggering deficit be avoided? I submit that it could. All will agree that with honest administration and the practice of economy it could have been greatly reduced. I will venture the statement that if the grafters and middlemen and patronage hunters and partisan committees had been driven out the Minister of Finance would not have to meet Parliament to-day in the humilating position he finds himself.
My hon. friend to-day says he could not interfere with contracts because the honour of Canada is at stake. That is a new
theory for hon. gentlemen opposite. They were hardly warm in their seats before they cancelled a contract made by the former Administration in my own constituency for the construction of a branch railway. The former Postmaster General has admitted in this House that he cancelled hundreds of contracts. A return was placed on the table last year showing that he cancelled no less than five hundred contracts for carrying the mails throughout this country. Many of these contracts were entered into after public tender and competition, and many of the men whose contracts were cancelled were ruined in the operation. But he claimed the right to do that on account of the fact that there is a clause in all Government contracts that enables the Government to cancel. It is a new doctrine for hon. gentlemen opposite that they cannot cancel contracts. Where was the " honour of Canada " in the cases of these five hundred contracts? Where was the honour of Canada in the case of the railway contract in my county.
Referring again to the deficit why should not this Government live within its income? The people are practising economy. They are endeavouring to live within their incomes^ The late Government lived within its income. If this Government cannot live within its income, permit me to suggest that they should be requested politely but firmly to step aside and make room for a Government that can. If you ask me to be specific, I will venture a few suggestions. In the discussion which took place in this House a few days ago, it was pointed out that the official staff appointed throughout this country since this Government came into power has been increased by the enormous number of ten thousand new officers. I know very well that explanations have been made, and I am quite willing to make allowances for all these explanations. But after the explanations had been submitted, after allowance has been made for what can be said on behalf of the ministers, we are forced to the conclusion that there was utter recklessness in securing positions for their partisans. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), whom I am glad to see in his place, is one of the most plausible of ministers in making explanations. But we all know the Minister of Customs. His method of appointing officers has been exposed at various times in this House. My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) gave one case that happened at Red Island in his

county a few days ago. The Minister of Customs dismissed an officer there because there was nothing for him to do; and then immediately afterwards appointed a party friend to do nothing at an increased salary -nearly twice as much as the former officer had. I pointed out a similar case in my own county. The hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) also exposed a case of that character in connection with the department of my hon. friend, in Antigonish. In that case it appears that a preventive officer was dismissed because there was nothing for him to do. The report of the inspector stated' that the officer had not struck a blow for nine years-and made no report to the Government for that length of time. In the face of that report the officer was very properly dismissed. But a party friend, one Moses Delorey, had to be looked after, and he insisted that he must have his reward. The Minister of Customs was up against it.
He is doing good work since.

So, what did the minister do ? He put Moses Delorey in the place of the dismissed officer. But the salary was not large enough, and in the face of the report of the inspector, he did not like to increase the salary. . So he appointed the same gentleman as an inspector of food. This " inspector of food " is residing in a country district where no inspection of food is carried on.
I did not do that.

No, but the Minister of Inland Revenue did. The return shows what was done. This man has for two years been drawing a salary as inspector of food; and outside the porridge pot in his own kitchen he has inspected nothing yet. In my own town, a few miles further west on the Intercolonial railway, a young man by the name of Cavanagh was dismissed from the customs service -by my hon. friend because there was no work for him to do.
That was a good reason.

Yes, if it was true, but whdt happened? In the place of this man, for whom he could find no work, my hon. friend appointed two men, at substantial salaries, to do the work Cavanagh had been doing. Similar instances could be found all along the three thousand miles between Cape Breton and British Columbia. In the face of examples of this kind, what is the

use of hon. gentlemen opposite trying to refute the accusation that they have increased their staff of officials to such an extent that their action has become a public scandal? The number of new appointments, after making allowance for resignations and dismissals, is placed at 10,000. One hon. gentleman estimated that these appointments would cost the country in salaries an average of $1,000 each. I think that that estimate is high. Some of these persons occupy important positions in the inside service, and, of course, draw correspondingly large salaries; but some are employed in the outside service at salaries which are not so high. But if we estimate the average salary at $500, that means $5,000,000 a year, or $16,000 a day, which is required to pay this increased official staff, the great majority of whom have been unnecessarily appointed to positions in the public service since hon. gentlemen opposite came into power. In view of these circumstances, what is the use of telling us that we are doing a patriotic act when we pay five cents additional a bottle on patent medicine, or two cents instead of one for a post card?
My second proposal is that the Government should abolish the middleman. I am glad the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is paying attention; he was the great critic of the middlemen when he sat on this side of the House. The middleman has had four fat years.

He had about fifteen
when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power.
of additional employees in order to collect an income tax. The hon. Minister of Customs himself figures in the list of appointments to the extent of 1,649 new officials.

That is not correct.
The hon. gentleman is not stating that correctly.
Substracting from that the number who died or were dismissed.
Yes.
There was a large increase was there not?
I said there was an increase but the hon. gentleman did not explain it correctly in the first instance.
My hon. friend did not wait for my explanation, after we make all allowances, there is a very large increase.
But there has been a very large increase in the revenue and new offices have been opened.
At present there is a very large decrease in the revenue.
No there is not, the revenue is increasing now.
It is increasing for the last month but that is only temporary, the decrease has been very marked for the whole of last year.
No, it has not.

Well then, the hon. gentleman's returns are not correct, my proposal is that the Minister of Customs could furnish a staff of men throughout this country who could collect the income tax without burdening the country with a new set of officers. There is one thing I would like about the income tax, it would afford some of those millionaires in Toronto and Montreal who have been accustomed for many years to shout loyalty, an opportunity to do something more substantial for their country than singing God save the King and waving the flag.
I wish to enter my protest against the 7i per cent increase in the general customs tariff. My chief reason is that it will increase the cost of living, which is already too high. It will not produce much revenue, it will put perhaps $3 in the pockets of the combines for every dollar it will into the treasury of the country. Besides it is done without any discrimination, no account is taken of the large number of articles of which there is no importation. These articles are taxed just the same and

from them not a dollar will come into the treasury of the country. A very large amount will be extracted from the pockets of the people by this means. Take, for example, the item of unbarked marlin, a kind of twine that is used on the coast of the maritime provinces by the fishermen for making lobster traps. Under the old Government that twine was admitted free. Under the present Government it is taxed 25 per cent.

There has been no
change in the tariff there, the hon. member knows that well.
My hon. friend knows too that he put a different construction on that item of the tariff since he came into office.

The tariff schedule itself shows it, but at the present time there is none of that cordage imported into Canada. That is a statement that my hon. friend will not deny. It is completely controlled by the cordage combine at Halifax or Montreal, wherever its headquarters are. The consequence is that the 25 per cent is at present squeezed out of the fishermen of the country and no cordage is imported. What will happen under the new tariff? It has come out during one of the discussions in this House that the Conservative party issued a pamphlet claiming that they

knew about the war for some two years before the war took place and that we innocent people on this side of the House did not know anything about it, that we could not recognize an emergency when we saw it. All I can say in reply is that if they really did know, there is no parallel in all history for their conduct unless it be the well known case of Nero who kept on fiddling while Rome was burning. When the crash came they were totally unprepared, both by land and sea. They had allowed the barnacles to accumulate on the bottom of the Niobe in Halifax. She was partly dismantled; some of her machinery was stored in a warehouse on a wharf in the dockyard. The officers had been encouraged to desert. The officers of the Naval Department were engaged in preparing a book on how to cook fish instead of preparing for war. A few days before war broke out the departmental report for the year was issued. I received my copy of the departmental report on the 6th day of August, just two days after the war broke out. I opened it eagerly to find whether the naval defence which we had in this country was in a good state of preparation. On the eighth page of the book I found the following:
Owing to the decision of the Government not to continue H.M.C. ships Niobe and Rainbow in full commission, the course of exercise and training for these ships has been discontinued and they are at present manned by nucleus crews.
That is what I found in the Naval report issued about the time war broke out. A few days after they got very busy in the dockyard at Halifax. A force of men was put on, a double shift was set to work, the ship was refitted and prepared for sea. That was the condition of our naval vessels when war broke out. What, let me ask, was the condition of the militia? Was it any better? The Militia Department, on an expenditure of about $12,000,000 during the previous fiscal year, was in very little better shape than the navy. The treasury was empty; the Finance Minister had been scraping the bottom of the pot for months before the war came. There was no clothing for the troops, no boots were ready for the soldiers. It has come out in the investigation that there was not even a specification in the department to tell what kind of boots a soldier should have for active service. There were no blankets, and socks were as scarce as blankets. Even the camp at Valcartier was not ready, the stumps had to be taken out, it all had to be cleared and drained and a water supply put in. There was absolutely
nothing ready but a long list of honorary colonels. Yet we are told that these gentlemen knew all about the war two years before it broke out! At the time of the Boer war some years ago, with a yearly expenditure of only $1,700,000 on militia, the country was much better-prepared than it was on this occasion. Permit me to remind hon. gentlemen opposite of the promptness with which the country responded in the case of the Boer war. The president of the Transvaal Republic declared war against Great Britain on the 9th day of October, 1899. On the 30th day of October of the same year, just 21 days afterwards, the steamship Sardinian was sailing down the St. Lawrence bearing the first contingent to a distant part of the world to fight for the flag, the men all ready and equipped. That is the way' the late Government met the emergency in 1899, not, of course, on such a large scale-

Could the hon. gentleman
tell how many men were sent at that time?

I have not the number here. I do not pretend it was anything like the same number as has been despatched at the present time; but I am pointing out that the Department of Militia, as managed and controlled by the late minister (Sir Frederick Borden), was in a state of preparation to respond to the call of war, and in the short space of three weeks he was able at least to do something; whereas the present department was not able to do anything in anything like that space of time. Let me suggest that my hon. friends will do well to suppress that pamphlet that has now become so well known and notorious, if they have not done so. If not, it is bound to do harm to them. The Canadian voter is the last man in the world to tolerate incompetence, especially at such a critical time in the country's history as the present.
I am glad to see that the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) is in his seat; I want to have just one word with him. We are ready to discuss that question at all times. My hon. friend poses as a philosopher, and I am free to admit that there is a thin veneer of philosophy outside of his outside skin.
But when you scratch him you find a Tory; and a Tory of that type that is peculiar to the province of Ontario, the type that

relies more on kindling prejudices against my honoured leader than on the justice of their cause. The word "may" did not suit him. In that word he saw a deep plot to wreck the Empire; and he wanted some word like "shall" or "must," I suppose, substituted for "may." He had no faith in the Canadian people. That is what was underneath the suggestion he made in that speech.
It is only a portion of the Canadian people that I have no faith in.

That is what was at the bottom of his suggestion. It is the same old Tory heresy that, in the early part of last century, placed his party against the granting of responsible government to this country; it is the same spirit that placed his party in England against granting selfgovernment to the Boers a few years ago; the same spirit that, a few months ago, almost turned the British Isles into an armed camp over the question of home rule for Ireland. I am sorry that that spirit still lives in the backwoods of West Peter-boro. But, suppose we had put the word "must" in. Do you think that would have made any difference? Would it have been respected by the present Government? Suppose we had put the word "must" in the British Preference Act. Would that have prevented my hon. friend the Minister of Finance from driving a horse and cart through it at the present time? Certainly not. My hon. friend knows that very well. But of course I am well aware that that speech of his was for consumption in West Peterboro. It is a well known fact in this country that he won his last election there on a bogus cry. He has practically admitted it in the House.
I appeal to the House against such an assertion as that. He has no right to say that I admitted such a thing in the House. The statement is false.
I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker. I say it is not false. I say it is true, and I can prove it by the records of the House.

Was he not well aware of that? But in face of the knowledge of that fact, he made the promise to his electors that, if elected, he would see that a uniform marriage law was passed for this country. Has he fulfilled the pledge he gave?
I do not run the whole House.

Has he attempted to
carry it out? He was well aware at the time he made it that he could not carry it out. He must have been aware of it. And now he is trying to stir up another question that he expects will do service for him in the backwoods of the same riding. I think I have dealt sufficiently with that question.
I do not wish to detain the House any longer; so, to sum up:
1.	I am cordially in favour of the proposed war loan. I am also in favour of such taxation as may be necessary to meet the interest on the war loan. I am prepared along with my colleagues on this side cordially to support any measure that will enable the Government to give effective assistance to the Empire in the supreme crisis through which it is now passing. To quote from my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), " millions for war, but not a dollar for graft."
2.	I am opposed to the 7i per cent increase in the general tariff because it is levied without discrimination. It will bear most heavily on those classes of the community least able to pay. It will not produce any substantial amount of revenue, and it cannot fail to enrich the combines.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate for the first time in the debates of this House, and I trust that I shall not transgress any of its rules. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Sinclair), and yesterday I listened with an especial interest to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), because, from the views he has enunciated on previous occasions in this House, and the stand he has taken as a free trader and a Cobdenite, I knew that he was a lucid and clear speaker. I am not sure, however, that my views on the question of protection have been changed by hearing the able remarks of the hon. gentleman. I knew that he had lived in the old land, where free trade' has for so long stood the test of time and given such satisfactory results. I am also not unmindful of the fact that the great German Empire and the great country to the south of us have, by protection, on entirely different systems, built up their trade and grown wealthy, possibly to an even greater extent than the Motherland herself. I believe that conditions in the old land make free trade the desirable policy for that country to pursue. But so far as Canada is concerned, there has never since protection was adopted been submitted to the people of this country an alternative fiscal policy which met with their approval, or which they were prepared to try out. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has referred to the panacea which the Government of the day applied to this country in 1911, in order to try and relieve our people from the ills that, in the Government's opinion, existed at that time -a time when the revenues of this country	were	buoyant,	and thecountry	in a	prosperous	condition.
Our hon. friends, in their wisdom, thought it good policy to undo the splendid structure that had been built up through the years under protection by casting in their lot with the United States, and opening up to them the markets of this splendid coun-50
try. I am glad that the hon. gentleman has given us the opportunity of considering that question of reciprocity again, and I can only say that if it should be the desire of the Opposition to discuss with the people again the same subject the Government are prepared to take the issue to the people, and I have no doubt the result will be the same as it has been since 1878. We have had similar policies enunciated at different periods in our history since 1878, and they have been submitted to the people. It seems to me that hon. gentlemen opposite take the view that the people do not really know what they want. They have had the question tested before by an appeal to the people and the country has supported the policy of protection.
The present situation is an extraordinary one. Nothing like it has ever at any time faced us in this country, and as hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have expressed their views on financial affairs as they are now, they seem to want to impress on the country and to try to convince themselves-although I cannot believe that they are convinced-that the great war now raging is responsible only for the amount of monejfthat we actually . expend in aid of the military that we send to help the Mother Country. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite do not believe any such thing. Surely they do not believe that the conditions of war are not responsible for the decreasing revenues of this country, or that there are not losses to the country resulting from the war conditions in Europe which are entirely aside from the expenses that will be incurred in equipping the forces we are sending to the front. The failure of so many intelligent citizens to realize and appreciate the tremendous effect of this war on finance, commerce and industry throughout the whole world is to me surprising.
The world's population to-day is estimated at 1,620,000,000 people, and of these 925,000,000 reside in the countries and their colonies affected by this war. The total area of the globe, exclusive of the polar regions, is about 52,000,000 square miles, and of this the countries engaged in the war represent an area of 28,500,000 square miles. Five continents are engaged more or less in the fighting. The greatest . wars of the past centuries were but trifling as compared with this mighty conflict. To-day armies aggregating 15,000,000 of the flower of the world's manhood have been summoned from field,



forest, mine, and factory. The great armies of England, France, Germany, Austria and Russia are facing each other in deadly combat along a battle line of over 1,000 miles. The war has already cost $8,500,000,000, it having been in progress for six months, and that represents an expenditure of $17,000,000,000 a year, or $47,000,000 a day. The world's trade is estimated at $40,000,000,000, and of this total the nations at war and their colonies represent $25,000,000,000. The commerce and finance of the whole world are so closely related and interdependent that it might be said that the arteries of the whole world are as closely associated as the arteries of the human body, and yet with these conditions prevailing in the great countries of Europe hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House virtually tell us that these conditions are in no way responsible for the shrinking revenues. The war has driven the powerful German marine off t'he high seas, and the foreign trade of Germany, Austria and Belgium, representing 22 per cent of the trade of the whole world, has practically vanished. These countries did with our country, as well as with the United States, a large volume of trade. Importation from these countries has absolutely vanished. That, necessarily, must diminish the revenue of Canada. Many of the agencies of transportation have been destroyed. Trade routes being deranged, demoralization and partial destruction in every branch of commercial and industrial activity is in evidence. During the year England's exports decreased by $475,000,000 and her imports by $355,000,000 making a total decrease in her foreign trade of $830,000,000. Notwithstanding her enormous importation of food stuffs her imports in Janu-5 p.m. ary last fell off $3,000,000 and her exports for the same month decreased $98,000,000. We know that in England large numbers of men have been withdrawn from the factory and the farm to fight in the trenches of France in defence of the Empire and that there is to some extent a dearth of labour in the larger factories and industries of England which are employed very fully at the present time. It is not surprising that it should be so. Belgium's trade of $1,500,000,000 is gone entirely and her fields are laid bare.
Going back a little beyond the present conditions I asked a question of my hon. friend from Guysborough last night which he did not answer. The question was if my hon. friend did not know that a war existed in the year 1912 and that the conditions 
brought About by reason of the war were conditions that led to the stagnation and to the interruption of commercial activity throughout the whole world. I referred to the Balkan war. The Balkan war, was a live, active war in that year and as a result of that war $450,000,000 of the capital of the world was obliterated. The increased outlay by armaments for the war and the gradual rise in the world's standard of prices, were the chief factors contributing to the financial depression of the time being. If hon. gentlemen wanted to be fair they would not condemn the fiscal policy of this country which for so many years has justified its existence and has been the source of a large revenue, and a source of strength in the development of our many industries. They would not deride that policy which the public six or seven times had endorsed as the correct policy of this country, nor blame the policy of protection for the conditions that prevailed at that time, which, -were, as hon. gentlemen must know, directly due to the world disturbance in finance and commerce. Reciprocity was the panacea suggested by my hon. friends. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) said last night:	.
We all - recognize that Canada is passing through a period of hard times. We may differ about the cause. Statesmen on this side of the House saw the depression coming prior to 1911, and they endeavoured to provide for it by opening new markets for Canadian products. Their efforts were frustrated, and Canada is having a taste of the depression that existed prior to 1896.
The hon. gentleman seemed at that time to have a vision of the future, a thing that hon. gentlemen opposite have not been troubled with in the past, because if they had that clear vision of what would come as the result of submitting that policy to the people of this country, they would have preferred the honour of serving their country as leaders in this House to going down to ignominious defeat as the result of submitting that policy to the people. If hon. gentlemen opposite wish to challenge the Government again on that issue, I am sure we shall be prepared to meet them in the country, and I have no doubt as to what the result will be when the question is submitted again to the people.
Our friends have to some extent derided the campaign, as we may call it, of *patriotism and production. I have even heard hon. gentlemen, who are interested in matters of agriculture and who represent agricultural districts, ridicule this policy. It will be an unfortunate thing for

this country if the time ever comes when a man engaged in agricultural production thinks there is nothing more to learn. I have the honour to represent a district which is peculiarly an agricultural one. In fact, I have not in the whole constituency even an incorporated village of any kind. My constituents are a very intelligent and progressive people. The Ontario Government has established in my county a district representative of the Department of Agriculture. It is the farmers who are progressive and enterprising, and who wish to be up-to-date who read the literature sent out and who attend the lectures that are given by that representative. A patriotism-and-production meeting was held in my district last month. At that meeting I learned from the district representative in our country of the splendid results obtained by our young men in what was called the acre-profit competition in the province of Ontario last year. In my own district, in the county of Middlesex, there were three farmers' sons, one of whom, as the result of the information he had obtained and the interest he had manifested in the lectures, was able in the competition to produce from one acre 501 bushels of potatoes, at a cost of $32.50, which were sold at 40 cents per bushel, giving a profit of $168 per acre. The other two boys from the same district were within ten bushels of these results. Each of those three boys produced an average of over $160 clear profit per acre as a result of the effort they had put forth in intensive production. The campaign, as the matter has been laid before the people, is encouraging them, not so much to a greater acreage as to a better production. The great problem is that of labour. Until that problem can be solved it will 'be difficult to increase production. The farmers of our country arfe working late and early, and are unable to procure sufficient labour. Notwithstanding that, I do not think any one denies that it is quite within the bounds of possibilities to apply more science to the development of agriculture, and by that, and by a little better tillage, to produce larger results on the same acreage.
There are three ways in which a farmer can increase production: first, by the application of increased labour; secondly, by the application of more intelligent a*nd scientific methods, and thirdly, by application of increased capital. I do not say that these three are entirely independent of each other. On the contrary, they are very closely connected. No one of them can be applied by itself alone. Each carries with it the necessity in some measure 58!
of both of the others.	Pure bred
stock, tile drains, improved buildings -all these things make	for better
production and essential pre-requisites for them is capital. The tendency of the whole financial world is to draw capital away from the farms. We find in all the small towns the banks establishing branches. The object of this is to collect the savings of the farmers and to distribute them in the commercial centres, applying the money to commerce and industry. This is the natural thing to do but works injury to farmers themselves who used increased capital for their operations. It cannot be denied, however, that agriculture is awakening to higher and to greater possibilities. The situation within the Empire in this world crisis calls upon our people for increased production. The people in this country are largely responding to that call. To fulfil these requirements, to meet the urgent demands of the Empire, the present need is for a large increase in the amount of capital available for rural credit on conditions suitable for agricultural enterprises? What in view of the situation ds required? What can be suggested by way of remedy? It is an economic certainty that every enterprise promptly responds to the magic touch of prosperity. Let the farmer have an experience of this, and you will see agriculture expand. Better returns to the farmer need not mean higher prices to the consumer owing to improved marketing, improved methods of transportation and storage facilities, not operated in the interest of the railways and the middleman, but in the interests of the producers and consumers. If scientific production is a good thing, then why not scientific marketing and scientific distribution? We cannot enlarge our farming activities unless the means to supply the capital is provided.
The question of credit for farmers is one which I think is of greatest importance. This is one of the problems that, I hope, this. Government will be able to meet. We are told, when a subject of this kind is presented, that it offers difficulties. But in spite of the difficulties the situation has been grappled with in the United States. A movement was commenced over a year ago to meet the growing needs for extended rural credits. A commission was appointed under the authority of Congress to go abroad and make a study of this whole matter, especially the organization and operation of rural credit associations in Europe. On its return the commission made a report, and, as a result, a Bill was introduced in both Houses of Congress embodying the ideas and plans of this com-

mission. This is called the Moss-Fletcner Bill. The McCumber Knral Credit Bill was later introduced as an alternative plan; and finally the Bulkley-Hollis Bill, an amendment to the Agricultural Appropriation Bill, was the one which met the approval of the Banking and Commerce Committee of tire Senate and was reported to the House of Representatives by a committee of that body. So the Bill has made good advance.
Some plan should be devised to enable farmers to organize co-operative credit associations throughout Canada with the assistance of the Government given under proper safeguards. The matter would imply using of the credit of the Government in a business-like way to reduce the enormous interest the farmers now have to pay. The great difference between the credit required for farmers and the credit required for ordinary commercial purposes is that the farmer requires a loan for a longer period than the ordinary commercial or industrial loan is expected to run. The application for credit should be supported by the Government in such a way as will give to the farmer, under proper safeguards, the assistance of the Government. That, to my mind, will go further to solve the problem of production and the problem of labour on the farm than anything else. It is of primary importance, above all other things. The interests of the farmer imperative^ demand that we should have legislation extending direct Government aid to the tiller of the soil. Cases have come within my own observation, and in my own township, of farmers with a large area of grazing land, but without the- capital to buy the necessary stock, and so their land goes to waste. I have seen more failures, I think, directly as a result of the want of capital to carry on the work of farming than from any other cause affecting my own district. I do not say that there are many who are in that unfavourable position. In fact they are comparatively few, because the farmers of that, district are progressive. And I find that the most progressive farmers there are those who do not sell their grain at the first price the market will give them after threshing, but they feed that grain to the stock on the farm, and so, as they say, their grain leaves the farm on the hoof. These are the men who are making a success of farming in our district.
Now, I have said there are difficulties in this matter. They have had difficulties to face in their efforts to solve this question in the United States. Sam Warren defines

difficulty as being only a word indicating the degree of strength requisite for accomplishing particular objects; a mere notice of the necessity for exertion; a bugbear to children and fools, but only a stimulus to men. There may be difficulties surrounding this question, but I believe that the more the problem is pressed upon the Government, the sooner a way will be found to solve it. I believe that Agriculture should be the most important department of the whole Government. We have our experimental farms, as we call them, in different parts of the country. And while these accomplish a good deal, in my humble opinion, the system of appointing district representatives in the various communities where they can become practically the agriculturists' doctors, right among the farmers themselves, is accomplishing a great r measure of good even than the work of the experimental farms. I hope the time will come when agriculture will be deemed of so much importance in this country that in every county at least, if not in every township, we may have a demonstration farm right in the midst of our people, which can be carried on with profit, and which will arouse the interest of the farmers in the most up-to-date and scientific methods of agriculture.
It has been stated, and it seems most unfortunate if true, that in Ontario, notwithstanding the enormous production of that province, they are not producing half of what the farms are capable of producing. I have given a good deal of thought to this matter and have discussed it with our representative including hon. gentlemen who are here representing eonstituentencies in the great West and who are endeavouring to make a good living out of farming in that country. I believe the time will come when they will follow the information that can be given in their agricultural schools in their several districts, and when the farmers there will not sell their oats at 25 cents a bushel and their barley at 30 and 35 cents, nor will they sell their wheat at the ridiculously low prices that have prevailed, but will feed their grain to stock and send it off on the hoof so that a twenty-five cent bushel of oats will represent a dollar or a dollar and ten cents before it leaves the farmer's hands. Our friends on the other side constantly complain of the tariff. But I believe the time will come when they will get interested in these lines. When the great West becomes a leading industrial district the demand from that

country for extensive changes in the tariff will entirely disappear.
In regard to the patriotism and production campaign throughout the country, I desire to say a word though the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) is not here. I would respectfully say that I think the campaign would have been productive- of even better results if the advertising campaign had preceded the meetings. I believe that the information gathered by the Department of Agriculture and issued in bulletins from time to time does not accomplish its full purpose, because the means of distribution is not what it should be. We have discussed this in the agricultural committee of this House and have not been able to suggest a method which would give the best distribution for this literature which, properly distributed, would he so valuable to the farmers of this country. I have thought, and still think, that it would be a good plan if bound catalogues of the publications of the department were in every rural reading library throughout the country. Then the man who is interested in live stock, the man who is interested in horticulture, the man who is interested in field crops, may send for the particular literature dealing with the special branch of agriculture he is particularly interested in.
I want to touch briefly on the matter of reciprocity, because that subject may, perchance, be a live issue when another appeal is made to the people. The inconsistency of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with this matter is amusing. I have a clipping from the Winnipeg Telegram in which reciprocity is recommended because eggs in Minneapolis are only 29 cents a dozen while in Winnipeg they are from 35 to 45 cents a dozen; because butter in Minneapolis is from 29 to 34 cents a pound, while in Winnipeg it is from 30 to 40 cents a pound. In the last reciprocity campaign hon. gentlemen opposite attempted to convince the people of cities and industrial communities on the one hand that the effect of reciprocity would be to lower to them the prices of these commodities, and on the other hand, that the farmer would get a better market on the other side for his produce. Hon. gentlemen were so inconsistent in the matter of reciprocity that they could not interest the people in it. It has been said that protection is foolish, and that if it were abandoned the country would he better off. But if it were not for the duties which keep them away, would American capital and American manufacturers invest half a billion dollars in establishing industries all over our country? Almost every member of this House has within his own constituency evidence of the fact that American manufacturers are establishing branches in Canada. My hon. friend the member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) probably knows better than any one else what the effect of reciprocity would be upon the large industrial district of which his constituency is a part. You cannot convince the farmers of that district that the markets of Detroit are better for his produce than the home market. He has the big markets of London, Toronto, and other places, and to these markets, taking advantage of the protection which he is afforded, he may ship his vegetables and other produce. The automobile industry in my hon. friend's constituency has grown to enormous proportions; notwithstanding the financial pressure which exists at the present time, it is expanding rapidly. The question naturally resolves itself into an inquiry as to what would he the benefit of reciprocity to the farmers. It has been repeated time and again-and it certainly must be evident to any hon. gentleman in this House-that a market that produces a surplus of 300,000,000 bushels of wheat cannot be the natural market for the products of this country.
I 'believe that hon. gentlemen opposite look upon the Globe as orthodox. I have a clipping from that journal of the issue of February 13, which says:
The price of Canadian wheat is fixed not in Winnipeg but in Liverpool. The price of cattle and hogs on this side of the border cannot long remain materially above that of food animals in the United States. Whatever is needed to turn the stream of settlement to the land should be done cheerfully and with the good-will of all classes of the community. Ontario's prosperity, like that of the Dominion at large, must spring from the presence on the farms of contented and prosperous food producers.
